connection: Session 26 introduced Task, Task<T>, Task.FromResult, async, and await through AsyncFlowExperiments. Production repositories and services remain synchronous. Session 27 compares sequential and concurrent flow using simulated waiting in the permanent ScratchPad notebook.
objectives: Explain when calling an asynchronous method starts its work and returns a Task.
Recognize that immediately awaiting one operation before calling the next creates sequential flow.
Create two independent Task<string> values before awaiting either operation.
Use Task.WhenAll with two explicitly named Task<string> values.
Distinguish concurrent asynchronous flow from parallel CPU execution.
Choose sequential flow when operations depend on order or share constrained resources.

visuals.title: Sequential flow crosses one bridge at a time
visuals.explanation: Start employee 1, await employee 1, then start employee 2 and await employee 2. The second operation does not exist while the first await is incomplete.

visuals.title: Concurrent flow places both orders first
visuals.explanation: Call the first operation and keep its Task, call the second and keep its Task, then await both. Both independent waits may now overlap.

visuals.title: Task.WhenAll is one finish line for two Tasks
visuals.explanation: Task.WhenAll returns a combined Task that completes after both supplied Task<string> values complete. Awaiting it returns a string array in supplied-Task order.

visuals.title: Concurrency overlaps waiting; parallelism overlaps execution
visuals.explanation: The experiment uses Task.Delay to simulate waiting. It does not prove that CPU work ran simultaneously or that another thread was created.

preQuiz.prompt: If the first asynchronous operation is immediately awaited, has the second operation started?
preQuiz.explanation: The second method call has not executed yet, so its operation and Task do not exist.

preQuiz.prompt: What normally happens when an async method is called?
options: It starts executing and returns a Task when it reaches incomplete waiting
It always creates a new thread
It waits for every other async method first
preQuiz.explanation: Calling starts the method. Its Task represents the method's eventual completion.

preQuiz.prompt: Does concurrent asynchronous work guarantee multiple threads?
preQuiz.explanation: Concurrency means lifetimes can overlap. It does not guarantee parallel threads or CPU execution.

concept.title: Sequential starts the second operation later
paragraphs: An async method begins when it is called. If code immediately awaits the first call, execution does not reach the second call until the first Task completes.

Sequential flow is appropriate when the second operation depends on the first, order matters, a rate limit applies, shared mutable state is involved, or a resource can handle only one operation at a time.
concept.code:
string firstName = await LoadEmployeeNameAsync(1, 300);
string secondName = await LoadEmployeeNameAsync(2, 100);

concept.title: Concurrent starts both independent operations first
paragraphs: Calling LoadEmployeeNameAsync without immediately awaiting it starts the method and returns Task<string>. Calling it a second time creates another operation before either Task is awaited.
This pattern is appropriate only when the operations are independent and safe to overlap. Concurrent does not mean parallel, and async does not automatically create a thread.

concept.title: Task.Delay makes waiting visible without pretending it is production I/O
paragraphs: Task.Delay simulates an incomplete wait so the console can show when each operation starts and finishes. It is not a repository call and does not create a dedicated background thread.

The different delays make employee 2 usually finish first during the concurrent observation. That completion order is not a general guarantee and is not a precise performance test. The lesson demonstrates overlapping waiting, not parallel CPU execution.

concept.title: Reading the Task.WhenAll signature
paragraphs: IntelliSense may show Task.WhenAll<TResult>(params Task<TResult>[] tasks). TResult is string in this call because each supplied argument is Task<string>.
Task.WhenAll returns one combined Task. Awaiting that combined Task produces string[]. The array preserves the order of the supplied Tasks, not the order in which they finished.

concept.title: Restaurant-orders analogy
paragraphs: Sequential: place the first restaurant order, wait until it is ready, and only then place the second order. Concurrent: place both independent orders first, then wait until both are ready.
The kitchen might use one worker or several workers. The analogy shows overlapping work and waiting; it does not guarantee parallel execution.

concept.title: Optional advanced side-lab outline — Generalize and test concurrency
paragraphs: This optional follow-up is not required for Session 27. It can later generalize two explicit Tasks into IEnumerable<int>, LINQ Select, a Func<int, Task<string>> load delegate, and Task.WhenAll over a generated sequence.

A later testing-focused version can introduce TaskCompletionSource, in-flight counters, and deterministic gates. Those concepts are intentionally excluded from the primary lab so they do not hide the basic start-first-versus-await-first decision.

list.text: Select calls an async load delegate for each ID
TaskCompletionSource gates and counters prove overlap without timing guesses

lab.title: Observe Sequential and Concurrent Waiting
lab.objective: Call the same two independent asynchronous operations sequentially and concurrently, then observe when each operation starts and finishes.
lab.task: Create a distinct Session 27 experiment that uses short simulated delays to make sequential and concurrent start/finish order visible.
lab.startingCondition: Session 26 created src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/Session26/AsyncFlowExperiments.cs and awaits it from ScratchPad Program.cs. Production repositories and services remain synchronous.

steps.text: In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, create folder Session27 and file src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/Session27/SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs. Setup code: add a comment identifying the Session 27 comparison.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, declare public sealed class SequentialConcurrentExperiments. public lets Program.cs create it; sealed prevents inheritance from this focused experiment class.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside SequentialConcurrentExperiments, add public async Task RunAsync() with a temporary throw. Task means eventual completion without a returned result; async permits await and does not create a thread.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside SequentialConcurrentExperiments but outside RunAsync, add private async Task<string> LoadEmployeeNameAsync(int employeeId, int delayMilliseconds) with a temporary throw. private keeps the helper inside this experiment; Task<string> means it eventually produces a string.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside LoadEmployeeNameAsync, replace the throw: print Starting employee and the ID, await Task.Delay(delayMilliseconds), print Finished employee and the ID, then return Employee plus the ID. Task.Delay is simulated waiting, not a repository call or parallel CPU proof.
From the csharp-practice-working solution folder, build project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad before adding the comparison methods.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside SequentialConcurrentExperiments but outside the existing methods, add private async Task RunSequentialAsync() with a temporary throw.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside RunSequentialAsync, replace the throw: call and immediately await employee 1 with 300 milliseconds, then employee 2 with 100 milliseconds; store both names and print them. Because the first call is immediately awaited, employee 2 has not started yet.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside SequentialConcurrentExperiments but outside the existing methods, add private async Task RunConcurrentAsync() with a temporary throw.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside RunConcurrentAsync, replace the throw by calling LoadEmployeeNameAsync for employee 1 without await and storing Task<string> firstTask, then doing the same for employee 2 in secondTask. Calling each async method starts it and returns a Task, so both have started before either is awaited.

Still inside SequentialConcurrentExperiments.RunConcurrentAsync, await Task.WhenAll(firstTask, secondTask), store the result in string[] names, then print the names. Signature reminder: TResult is string, both arguments are Task<string>, and the returned array follows supplied-Task order rather than completion order.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, folder Session27, file SequentialConcurrentExperiments.cs, inside RunAsync, remove the temporary throw. Print Sequential, await RunSequentialAsync, print Concurrent, then await RunConcurrentAsync.

In project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad, file src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.ScratchPad/Program.cs, after all earlier session calls, add a Session 27 heading, create SequentialConcurrentExperiments in sequentialConcurrentExperiments, and await RunAsync. Run ScratchPad and compare the messages; employee 2 will usually finish first concurrently, but completion order is not a general guarantee.
From the csharp-practice-working solution folder, build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln in Release and run the complete test suite without rebuilding. Open Solution Reveal only after both pass.
steps.code:
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: Sequential awaits each operation before starting the next. Concurrent creates both Tasks first and then awaits the combined Task.

lab.expectedBehavior:
Sequential
Starting employee 1
Finished employee 1
Starting employee 2
Finished employee 2
Results: Employee 1, Employee 2
Concurrent
Starting employee 1
Starting employee 2
Finished employee 2
Finished employee 1
Results: Employee 1, Employee 2

The different delays make employee 2 usually finish first concurrently. The lesson relies only on both start messages appearing before completion; it does not treat completion timing as a general guarantee.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can the two employee operations overlap in RunConcurrentAsync?
options: Both async methods are called and their Tasks stored before Task.WhenAll is awaited
postQuiz.explanation: Both operations have started before the combined Task is awaited. The delay lengths affect observation, not the reason overlap is possible.

options: When order, dependency, rate limits, shared state, or constrained resources matter
Only when a computer has one CPU core
postQuiz.explanation: Concurrency is a design choice for independent work, not an automatic improvement.

postQuiz.prompt: What does awaiting Task.WhenAll over two Task<string> values return?
options: A string array in supplied-Task order
postQuiz.explanation: The generic result type is string, so awaiting the combined Task produces string[].

reflections: At which exact line does employee 2 begin in sequential flow, and why has it not started earlier?
Why can employee 2 finish first concurrently while the names array still lists Employee 1 first?
Which real-world constraints would make you choose sequential flow even when overlap could be faster?
whatBreaks: Immediately awaiting firstTask before calling the second helper turns the concurrent method back into sequential flow. Removing await from Task.WhenAll lets RunConcurrentAsync finish before both operations are observed. Reusing the global name AsyncFlowExperiments would collide with Session 26 because this project currently has no namespaces separating those types.
summary: Calling and immediately awaiting one operation before calling the next creates sequential flow. Calling two independent async methods first creates two Tasks whose waits can overlap; Task.WhenAll returns a combined Task that completes after both. This is concurrency, not guaranteed parallel execution, and production remains synchronous.
